items.fix: Queue one utterance per paragraph (headline, then body paragraphs). Handle `onend` and `onerror` on each and reset state after the last. This also enables pause/resume, skip and highlighting. Tell the user when playback fails, in visible text and a polite live region. Test full playback in Chrome, Edge, Safari and Firefox, desktop and mobile, with default and network voices.
items.impact: Listeners relying on read-aloud (dyslexia, low vision, learning disabilities, low literacy, fatigue) may hear only the byline, the button label and the incorrect key points, then silence. Nothing says reading stopped, the button still shows pressed, and they never reach the correction.
items.problem: The whole article goes to the speech engine as one long utterance. In Chromium-based browsers long utterances are known to stop after about 15 seconds with some voices, often network voices, without an `end` or `error` event the page handles. Playback stops partway, usually before the body and always before the correction. The button stays at `aria-pressed="true"`. There is one `speak()` call, no chunking and no event handlers.

items.fix: Choose one pattern. Option 1: plain button without `aria-pressed`, label switching between "Listen to this article" and "Stop listening", with a polite live-region message. Option 2: keep `aria-pressed` with a fixed label such as "Read aloud" and show the state visibly (style plus the word "Playing"). Do not mix. Test with NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack, Dragon and Voice Control.
items.impact: Screen-reader, cognitive-disability and voice-control users (who would say "click Listen" to stop) are unsure how to stop the audio, or press again expecting a restart; label-only users are told the opposite of what the button does.
items.problem: Screen readers announce "Listen to this article, toggle button, pressed", which does not make clear whether it is playing or whether pressing again stops it. The visible label stays "Listen to this article" while playing, so stopping means pressing a button labelled "Listen". The toggle-button pattern says the label of an `aria-pressed` button must not change, so a label swap such as "Stop listening" would produce "Stop listening, toggle button, pressed". The script toggles `aria-pressed`; no state is styled or described.
items.where: article.html `<button type="button" id="listen" aria-pressed="false">Listen to this article</button>`
